idiom_name: Map<K, (A) -> R> handler map with ?.invoke ?: throw miss policy
implementation_notes: Kotlin makes both halves ordinary values: `val handlers: Map<Op, (Ctx, Int) -> Int> = mapOf(Op.ADD to { ctx, v -> ctx.acc + v })` and dispatch is `handlers[op]?.invoke(ctx, arg) ?: throw UnknownOpException(op)`. What replaces the classic structure is the stdlib map plus function types, with `getValue`, `getOrElse` and `getOrDefault` expressing the miss policy in one expression and enum keys keeping the key space explicit. When the discriminant is a closed `sealed interface`/`sealed class`, a `when` expression is checked for exhaustiveness by the compiler and no table is needed; keep the map when handlers are registered from several modules, come from configuration, or must be enumerated at runtime for help or diagnostics.
code_sketch:
val handlers: Map<Op, (Ctx, Int) -> Int> = mapOf(
    Op.ADD to { ctx, v -> ctx.acc + v },
    Op.SUB to { ctx, v -> ctx.acc - v },
)

fun dispatch(op: Op, arg: Int): Int =
    handlers[op]?.invoke(ctx, arg) ?: throw UnknownOpException(op)
pitfalls: `handlers[op]` returns null both when the key is absent and (with a nullable value type) when it is mapped to null, so keep handler types non-null and let null mean 'unregistered'.

Lambda entries capture variables: registering a lambda over a mutable var or a lateinit field makes every dispatch see the value at call time, which is rarely what the registration site looks like it does.

A `Map` interface is read-only to you but may be backed by a MutableMap another module mutates concurrently - publish with toMap()/buildMap or use ConcurrentHashMap when registration continues after startup.

Relying on `when` with an `else` branch reintroduces the silent default that exhaustiveness checking exists to prevent; when a table is the wrong shape, prefer a sealed hierarchy and a `when` without `else`.
